papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that reasoning behaviors in thinking LLMs are mediated by linear directions in the activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors extracted via difference of means and attribution patching.
papers.conclusion: Steering vectors provide a practical method for controlling reasoning behaviors in thinking models, opening new possibilities for fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Thinking models exhibit distinct reasoning behaviors such as backtracking, uncertainty estimation, and example testing.
These behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space.
Steering vectors extracted via difference of means can control these behaviors, increasing or decreasing their occurrence.
The steering approach works across different model architectures within the DeepSeek-R1-Distill family.
The method provides a practical tool for modulating reasoning capabilities in thinking models.
papers.limitation:
The automated annotation process using GPT-4o has occasionally produced false positives and false negatives in identifying reasoning patterns.
The generalization of these findings to other models that have undergone reward-based RL training instead of being fine-tuned on thinking models remains an open question.
future_direction: Developing more robust annotation methods, potentially incorporating multiple models or human validation.
Extending the research to a broader range of models to understand the universality of thinking mechanisms.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have led to the development of thinking language models that generate extensive internal reasoning chains before producing responses. While these models achieve improved performance, controlling their reasoning processes remains challenging. This work presents a steering approach for thinking LLMs by analyzing and manipulating specific reasoning behaviors in DeepSeek-R1-Distill models. Through a systematic experiment on 500 tasks across 10 diverse categories, we identify several reasoning behaviors exhibited by thinking models, including expressing uncertainty, generating examples for hypothesis validation, and backtracking in reasoning chains. We demonstrate that these behaviors are mediated by linear directions in the model's activation space and can be controlled using steering vectors. By extracting and applying these vectors, we provide a method to modulate specific aspects of the model's reasoning process, such as its tendency to backtrack or express uncertainty. Our approach offers practical tools for steering reasoning processes in thinking models in a controlled and interpretable manner. We validate our steering method using three DeepSeek-R1-Distill models, demonstrating consistent control across different model architectures.

papers.title: A Detailed Study of Interpretability of Deep Neural Network based Top Taggers
papers.research_question: How can we interpret deep neural network models for top quark jet tagging, and how can interpretability methods be used to improve model design?
papers.core_contribution: The paper studies interpretability of DNN-based top taggers, uncovers pitfalls of existing XAI methods, and proposes a new model (PFIN) that improves performance through interpretability-inspired design.
papers.conclusion: This work establishes a methodological paradigm to demonstrate the usage of XAI tools for day-to-day applications of DNNs and MLPs in high energy physics, and shows how interpretability can lead to improved model design.
papers.key_findings:
Different XAI methods (∆AUC, SHAP, LRP) can produce inconsistent feature rankings, and modifying LRP to differential relevance scores (MAD) yields more consistent results.
Correlations among input features can obscure interpretability, as seen in the MB8S model.
NAP diagrams reveal sparsity in network activations and can guide model reoptimization by removing inactive layers or neurons.
The proposed PFIN model, which incorporates pairwise particle interactions, outperforms baseline models in top tagging.
Latent space embeddings in PFN capture physical jet features and show disentanglement between jet classes.
future_direction: Adapting interpretability tools for more general data types and novel architectures like graph nets and transformers
papers.abstract: Recent developments in the methods of explainable AI (XAI) allow researchers to explore the inner workings of deep neural networks (DNNs), revealing crucial information about input-output relationships and realizing how data connects with machine learning models. In this paper we explore interpretability of DNN models designed to identify jets coming from top quark decay in high energy proton-proton collisions at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). We review a subset of existing top tagger models and explore different quantitative methods to identify which features play the most important roles in identifying the top jets. We also investigate how and why feature importance varies across different XAI metrics, how correlations among features impact their explainability, and how latent space representations encode information as well as correlate with physically meaningful quantities. Our studies uncover some major pitfalls of existing XAI methods and illustrate how they can be overcome to obtain consistent and meaningful interpretation of these models. We additionally illustrate the activity of hidden layers as Neural Activation Pattern (NAP) diagrams and demonstrate how they can be used to understand how DNNs relay information across the layers and how this understanding can help to make such models significantly simpler by allowing effective model reoptimization and hyperparameter tuning. These studies not only facilitate a methodological approach to interpreting models but also unveil new insights about what these models learn. Incorporating these observations into augmented model design, we propose the Particle Flow Interaction Network (PFIN) model and demonstrate how interpretability-inspired model augmentation can improve top tagging performance.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Catastrophic Forgetting in Large Language Models During Continual Fine-tuning
papers.research_question: What are the primary mechanisms driving catastrophic forgetting in large language models during continual fine-tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies three primary mechanisms of catastrophic forgetting in LLMs during sequential fine-tuning: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening around prior task minima.
papers.conclusion: Catastrophic forgetting in LLMs is driven by three interacting mechanisms (attention disruption, representational drift, loss landscape flattening), providing a mechanistic foundation for developing targeted continual learning strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 15-23% of attention heads, particularly in lower layers, undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, driving early forgetting.
Representational drift in intermediate layers, measured by CKA similarity, decreases by 0.32 to 0.47, indicating significant geometric changes.
Gradient interference, especially in query and key projection matrices, strongly predicts forgetting severity (correlation r=0.87).
The loss landscape around previous task minima flattens substantially (maximum Hessian eigenvalue drops from 147.3 to 34.2), making recovery difficult.
These three mechanisms interact and operate at different timescales, with attention disruption early, representational drift accumulating, and landscape flattening emerging later.
papers.limitation:
Experimental design focused on task sequences with clear boundaries, not continuous adaptation to gradually shifting distributions.
Examined forgetting over relatively short task sequences (4 to 6 tasks), while practical systems may encounter hundreds of sequential tasks.
Mechanistic analysis primarily characterized average behaviors across many model instances; understanding individual variability and rare failure modes remains important.
future_direction: Developing architecture modifications that inherently resist the identified forgetting mechanisms, such as attention heads with built-in stability constraints or intermediate layers with protected representational subspaces.
Designing optimization algorithms that explicitly manage gradient interference, representational drift, and landscape geometry during fine-tuning.
Creating diagnostic tools that monitor mechanistic signatures in real-time to prevent catastrophic forgetting before it occurs.
papers.abstract: Large language models exhibit remarkable performance across diverse tasks through pre-training and fine-tuning paradigms. However, continual fine-tuning on sequential tasks induces catastrophic forgetting, where newly acquired knowledge interferes with previously learned capabilities. Despite widespread observations of this phenomenon, the mechanistic understanding remains limited. Here, we present a comprehensive mechanistic analysis of catastrophic forgetting in transformer-based LLMs during sequential fine-tuning. Through systematic experiments across multiple model scales (109B to 400B total parameters) and task sequences, we identify three primary mechanisms driving forgetting: gradient interference in attention weights, representational drift in intermediate layers, and loss landscape flattening. We demonstrate that forgetting severity correlates strongly with task similarity (Pearson r = 0.87) and gradient alignment metrics. Our analysis reveals that approximately 15 to 23 percent of attention heads undergo severe disruption during fine-tuning, with lower layers showing greater susceptibility. These findings establish mechanistic foundations for developing targeted mitigation strategies in continual learning systems.

papers.title: Transcoder-based Circuit Analysis for Interpretable Single-Cell Foundation Models
papers.research_question: How can transcoders be used to extract interpretable decision-making circuits from single-cell foundation models, and do these circuits correspond to biological mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that applying transcoders to single-cell foundation models enables the extraction of biologically interpretable internal decision circuits, confirming the potential of this approach for mechanistic interpretability in computational biology.
papers.conclusion: Transcoders provide a viable method for extracting interpretable circuits from single-cell foundation models, opening new avenues for interpretability research in this domain, though manual interpretation remains a limitation.
papers.key_findings:
Transcoders can be successfully trained on the C2S model, capturing significant MLP functionality as shown by validation loss comparison.
Human evaluation of transcoder features revealed that 35% of randomly selected features were gene-level interpretable.
Extracted circuits for cell type classification include features corresponding to biologically relevant genes such as VWF, PTPRB, and SPARCL1.
The transcoder-replaced model has lower validation loss than a model with MLPs removed, indicating effective approximation.
Circuit tracing identifies computational paths involving attention and MLP features that contribute to predictions.
papers.limitation:
Biological interpretation of extracted circuits was performed manually, which is time-consuming and potentially subjective.
The choice of training dataset significantly impacts the features learned by transcoders, limiting generalizability.
future_direction: Develop automated interpretation methods to systematically map transcoder features to biological concepts.
Explore other datasets to reveal more general features and circuits across different biological contexts.
Develop novel methods to further enhance scFM interpretability and apply these techniques to discover new biological insights.
papers.abstract: Single-cell foundation models (scFMs) have demonstrated state-of-the-art performance on various tasks, such as cell-type annotation and perturbation response prediction, by learning gene regulatory networks from large-scale transcriptome data. However, a significant challenge remains: the decision-making processes of these models are less interpretable compared to traditional methods like differential gene expression analysis. Recently, transcoders have emerged as a promising approach for extracting interpretable decision circuits from large language models (LLMs). In this work, we train a transcoder on the cell2sentence (C2S) model, a state-of-the-art scFM. By leveraging the trained transcoder, we extract internal decision-making circuits from the C2S model. We demonstrate that the discovered circuits correspond to real-world biological mechanisms, confirming the potential of transcoders to uncover biologically plausible pathways within complex single-cell models.

papers.title: Learning Transformer Programs
papers.research_question: How can we train Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design, rather than reverse-engineering black-box models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method for training Transformers that are interpretable by design, which can be automatically converted into discrete, human-readable programs after training.
papers.conclusion: Transformer Programs represent a promising step towards building intrinsically interpretable machine learning models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer Programs can achieve reasonable performance on a variety of tasks, including algorithmic problems and NLP tasks, comparable to standard Transformers of similar size.
The learned programs are easy to interpret and can be analyzed using standard code analysis tools, such as debuggers, to understand model behavior and debug errors.
The method faces optimization challenges, especially when scaling to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths, and the learned programs can be non-intuitive.
papers.limitation:
Optimization challenges make it difficult to scale to larger vocabularies and sequence lengths.
The learned programs can be complicated and non-intuitive, differing from human-written solutions.
future_direction: Scaling Transformer Programs to larger models and more complex tasks.
Developing methods for automatically analyzing the resulting programs and imposing inductive biases for more interpretable programs.
papers.abstract: Recent research in mechanistic interpretability has attempted to reverse-engineer Transformer models by carefully inspecting network weights and activations. However, these approaches require considerable manual effort and still fall short of providing complete, faithful descriptions of the underlying algorithms. In this work, we introduce a procedure for training Transformers that are mechanistically interpretable by design. We build on RASP [Weiss et al., 2021], a programming language that can be compiled into Transformer weights. Instead of compiling human-written programs into Transformers, we design a modified Transformer that can be trained using gradient-based optimization and then automatically converted into a discrete, human-readable program. We refer to these models as Transformer Programs. To validate our approach, we learn Transformer Programs for a variety of problems, including an in-context learning task, a suite of algorithmic problems (e.g. sorting, recognizing Dyck languages), and NLP tasks including named entity recognition and text classification. The Transformer Programs can automatically find reasonable solutions, performing on par with standard Transformers of comparable size; and, more importantly, they are easy to interpret. To demonstrate these advantages, we convert Transformers into Python programs and use off-the-shelf code analysis tools to debug model errors and identify the "circuits" used to solve different sub-problems. We hope that Transformer Programs open a new path toward the goal of intrinsically interpretable machine learning.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding and validation of large AI models with SemanticLens
papers.research_question: How can we achieve automated explanation and validation of model components at scale to understand their inner knowledge and ensure alignment with human expectations?
papers.core_contribution: SemanticLens is a universal explanation method that embeds neural network components into the semantic space of a foundation model, enabling scalable search, description, comparison, and auditing of learned concepts for component-level understanding and validation.
papers.conclusion: By enabling component-level understanding and validation, SemanticLens helps mitigate the opacity of AI models, facilitating more reliable deployment in critical applications.
papers.key_findings:
SemanticLens enables text-based search to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, such as biases or data artefacts, in models like ResNet50v2.
It can describe and structure the internal knowledge of models through semantic embeddings, revealing clusters of concepts like animals and vehicles.
The method allows auditing of concept alignment with expected reasoning, detecting spurious correlations and measuring reliance on valid vs. spurious concepts.
In medical image analysis, SemanticLens identifies spurious components (e.g., scale bars, band-aids) and enables model correction via pruning or retraining, improving robustness.
It introduces interpretability measures (clarity, polysemanticity, redundancy) that correlate with human perception and vary across architectures and training regimes.
papers.limitation: Concepts may be distributed across several components, and the neural basis may not comprehensively capture all relevant concepts.
papers.abstract: Abstract Unlike human-engineered systems, such as aeroplanes, for which the role and dependencies of each component are well understood, the inner workings of artificial intelligence models remain largely opaque, which hinders verifiability and undermines trust. Current approaches to neural network interpretability, including input attribution methods, probe-based analysis and activation visualization techniques, typically provide limited insights about the role of individual components or require extensive manual interpretation that cannot scale with model complexity. This paper introduces SemanticLens, a universal explanation method for neural networks that maps hidden knowledge encoded by components (for example, individual neurons) into the semantically structured, multimodal space of a foundation model such as CLIP. In this space, unique operations become possible, including (1) textual searches to identify neurons encoding specific concepts, (2) systematic analysis and comparison of model representations, (3) automated labelling of neurons and explanation of their functional roles, and (4) audits to validate decision-making against requirements. Fully scalable and operating without human input, SemanticLens is shown to be effective for debugging and validation, summarizing model knowledge, aligning reasoning with expectations (for example, adherence to the ABCDE rule in melanoma classification) and detecting components tied to spurious correlations and their associated training data. By enabling component-level understanding and validation, the proposed approach helps mitigate the opacity that limits confidence in artificial intelligence systems compared to traditional engineered systems, enabling more reliable deployment in critical applications.

papers.title: Low-Complexity Probing via Finding Subnetworks
papers.research_question: Can a subtractive pruning-based probe (subnetwork probing) more faithfully detect linguistic properties encoded in a pre-trained model compared to traditional MLP probes, by being better at finding existing properties and worse at learning tasks on its own?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces subnetwork probing, a pruning-based method that finds a subnetwork within a frozen pre-trained model to perform a linguistic task, demonstrating it is more faithful to the model (higher accuracy on pre-trained, lower on random models) and Pareto-dominates MLP probes in accuracy-complexity tradeoff.
papers.conclusion: Subnetwork probing is a more faithful probing method than existing approaches for understanding what linguistic properties are encoded in pre-trained models, and it enables additional analysis through the subnetworks it discovers.
papers.key_findings:
Subnetwork probing achieves higher accuracy on the pre-trained model and lower accuracy on randomly initialized models compared to an MLP probe, indicating it is better at finding encoded properties and less capable of learning the task independently.
Subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing, achieving higher accuracy for any given probe complexity budget.
Analysis of the extracted subnetworks shows that lower-level linguistic tasks (e.g., part-of-speech tagging) are localized in lower layers of the model, reproducing findings from prior work.
future_direction: Applying neuron explainability techniques to the subnetworks discovered by the method.
papers.abstract: The dominant approach in probing neural networks for linguistic properties is to train a new shallow multi-layer perceptron (MLP) on top of the model's internal representations. This approach can detect properties encoded in the model, but at the cost of adding new parameters that may learn the task directly. We instead propose a subtractive pruning-based probe, where we find an existing subnetwork that performs the linguistic task of interest. Compared to an MLP, the subnetwork probe achieves both higher accuracy on pre-trained models and lower accuracy on random models, so it is both better at finding properties of interest and worse at learning on its own. Next, by varying the complexity of each probe, we show that subnetwork probing Pareto-dominates MLP probing in that it achieves higher accuracy given any budget of probe complexity. Finally, we analyze the resulting subnetworks across various tasks to locate where each task is encoded, and we find that lower-level tasks are captured in lower layers, reproducing similar findings in past work.

papers.title: RAVEL: Evaluating Interpretability Methods on Disentangling Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: To what extent can different interpretability methods successfully disentangle the roles of neurons in representing multiple high-level concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the RAVEL benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods on attribute disentanglement in language models, and proposes Multi-task Distributed Alignment Search (MDAS) which achieves state-of-the-art results, demonstrating the importance of distributed feature identification.
papers.conclusion: Presents the RAVEL benchmark for evaluating interpretability methods on attribute disentanglement, shows that Multi-task DAS achieves the best results, and releases the benchmark to drive future development of interpretability methods.
papers.key_findings:
Methods with counterfactual supervision (DBM, DAS, MDAS) achieve strong disentanglement scores, while unsupervised featurizers (PCA, SAE) struggle.
Multi-task supervision (MDBM, MDAS) improves isolation of attributes compared to single-task versions.
Some attribute pairs (e.g., country-language, latitude-longitude) are inherently difficult to disentangle in the model.
Attributes become gradually disentangled across transformer layers, with later layers showing higher disentanglement scores.
papers.limitation:
Results are based on Llama2-7B; different model architectures or training paradigms might favor different interpretability methods.
Intervention sites are limited to the residual stream at the last entity token, but attribute representations could be distributed across multiple tokens or layers.
future_direction: Instantiate RAVEL on new models to evaluate interpretability methods.
Explore different intervention sites beyond the residual stream at the last entity token.
papers.abstract: Individual neurons participate in the representation of multiple high-level concepts. To what extent can different interpretability methods successfully disentangle these roles? To help address this question, we introduce RAVEL (Resolving Attribute-Value Entanglements in Language Models), a dataset that enables tightly controlled, quantitative comparisons between a variety of existing interpretability methods. We use the resulting conceptual framework to define the new method of Multi-task Distributed Alignment Search (MDAS), which allows us to find distributed representations satisfying multiple causal criteria. With Llama2-7B as the target language model, MDAS achieves state-of-the-art results on RAVEL, demonstrating the importance of going beyond neuron-level analyses to identify features distributed across activations. We release our benchmark at https://github.com/explanare/ravel.

papers.title: Preserving Bilinear Weight Spectra with a Signed and Shrunk Quadratic Activation Function
papers.research_question: Can we design an activation function for Gated Linear Units (GLUs) that enables weight-based interpretability (via eigen-features) without sacrificing performance and data efficiency?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function for GLUs that preserves the weight structure properties of bilinear MLPs (enabling interpretability via eigen-decomposition) while achieving performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions.
papers.conclusion: Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS) is an activation function that enables the development of interpretable features via weight spectra while providing performance on par with, and in some scenarios better than, standard activation functions.
papers.key_findings:
SQS-GLU learns interpretable features, as shown by eigenvector decomposition of its weight matrices, similar to bilinear MLPs.
SQS achieves performance (loss, accuracy, perplexity) competitive with or better than ReLU, GELU, and SwiGLU on MNIST, Fashion MNIST, and Tiny Stories.
SQS converges faster and achieves lower loss than ReLU-GLUs and Bilinear MLPs on the image classification tasks.
The eigenvectors from SQS-GLU show high cosine similarity with those from Bilinear MLPs, indicating preserved interpretability.
SQS maintains computational efficiency comparable to other activation functions when implemented with specific hyperparameters.
papers.abstract: Understanding the inner workings of machine learning models is critical for ensuring their reliability and robustness. Whilst many techniques in mechanistic interpretability focus on activation driven analyses, being able to derive meaningful features directly from the weights of a neural network would provide greater guarantees and more computational efficiency. Existing techniques for analyzing model features through weights suffer from drawbacks such as reduced performance and data inefficiency. In this paper, we introduce Signed Quadratic Shrink (SQS), an activation function designed to allow Gated Linear Units (GLUs) to learn interpretable features without these drawbacks. Our experimental results show that SQS achieves performance competitive with state-of-the-art activation functions whilst enabling weight-based interpretability

papers.title: Locate, Steer, and Improve: A Practical Survey of Actionable Mechanistic Interpretability in Large Language Models
papers.core_contribution: This survey presents a structured framework for actionable mechanistic interpretability, categorizing methods into 'Locate, Steer, and Improve' to operationalize MI for model optimization in alignment, capability, and efficiency.
papers.conclusion: The survey advocates for shifting from passive observation to active intervention using the 'Locate, Steer, and Improve' pipeline to advance model optimization through mechanistic interpretability.
papers.limitation: the lack of robust evaluation frameworks to assess the faithfulness of localization and explanation methods
future_direction: Broadening the Architectural Scope
Integration with Cognitive Science
Theoretical Foundations
papers.abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) has emerged as a vital approach to demystify the opaque decision-making of Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing reviews primarily treat MI as an observational science, summarizing analytical insights while lacking a systematic framework for actionable intervention. To bridge this gap, we present a practical survey structured around the pipeline: "Locate, Steer, and Improve." We formally categorize Localizing (diagnosis) and Steering (intervention) methods based on specific Interpretable Objects to establish a rigorous intervention protocol. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this framework enables tangible improvements in Alignment, Capability, and Efficiency, effectively operationalizing MI as an actionable methodology for model optimization. The curated paper list of this work is available at https://github.com/rattlesnakey/Awesome-Actionable-MI-Survey.

papers.title: PURE: Turning Polysemantic Neurons Into Pure Features by Identifying Relevant Circuits
papers.research_question: Can we find and purify polysemantic neurons? How effective is PURE in disentangling representations compared to other approaches?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PURE, a post-hoc method to disentangle polysemantic neurons into multiple pure virtual neurons by identifying the active circuit for each feature.
papers.conclusion: PURE turns polysemantic neurons into multiple purer virtual neurons by identifying active circuits, resulting in more purified features than activation-based approaches and improving interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Polysemantic neurons exist in ResNet models and can be disentangled into pure features using circuit identification.
PURE effectively disentangles representations, leading to more interpretable virtual neurons compared to activation-based clustering.
PURE attributions are more aligned with CLIP embedding distances than activations, indicating better neuron-specific disentanglement.
PURE performs close to DINOv2 in terms of cluster separation while being computationally more efficient than DINOv2-based clustering.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation relies on foundational models (CLIP/DINOv2) as proxies for human interpretability, which may not perfectly align with human judgment.
PURE requires a partial backward pass for each neuron, making it computationally more demanding than activation-based methods.
future_direction: Evaluation in controlled settings or using human feedback for interpretability.
Ablation studies on clustering full circuits, different attribution methods, and clustering approaches.
Investigating advantages of purified units for XAI tools like concept-based explanations, concept discovery, probing, or model correction.
papers.abstract: The field of mechanistic interpretability aims to study the role of individual neurons in Deep Neural Networks. Single neurons, however, have the capability to act polysemantically and encode for multiple (unrelated) features, which renders their interpretation difficult. We present a method for disentangling polysemanticity of any Deep Neural Network by decomposing a polysemantic neuron into multiple monosemantic "virtual" neurons. This is achieved by identifying the relevant sub-graph ("circuit") for each "pure" feature. We demonstrate how our approach allows us to find and disentangle various polysemantic units of ResNet models trained on ImageNet. While evaluating feature visualizations using CLIP, our method effectively disentangles representations, improving upon methods based on neuron activations. Our code is available at https://github.com/maxdreyer/PURE.

papers.title: Unraveling the cognitive patterns of Large Language Models through module communities
papers.research_question: How are cognitive skills organized within Large Language Models (LLMs), and do they exhibit modular specialization similar to biological systems?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a network-based framework linking cognitive skills, LLM architectures, and datasets, finding that LLMs exhibit a distributed organization of cognitive skills within module communities, contrasting with the localized specialization in biological systems.
papers.conclusion: The study reveals that LLMs internalize cognitive skills in a distributed manner across module communities, suggesting that effective fine-tuning strategies should leverage network-wide dependencies and distributed learning dynamics rather than rigid modular interventions.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit a community structure in their modules that is associated with cognitive skills, but this structure does not align with predefined cognitive function categories.
Community-based fine-tuning induces the most substantial weight changes but does not yield a clear accuracy advantage over fine-tuning randomly selected modules or all modules.
Cognitive skills in LLMs are distributed across module communities, showing a pattern more akin to weak-localization architectures (e.g., avian brains) than the strong task-specific localization seen in the human brain.
Module communities within LLMs are tightly connected internally but also exhibit cross-community interactions, as measured by network metrics like participation coefficient and Z-score.
The distribution of skills across module communities is statistically independent of predefined cognitive categories, indicating a unique organizational principle in LLMs.
papers.limitation:
The abstract cognitive skills defined could be further refined to capture a more nuanced spectrum of human cognition.
Computational constraints influenced model selection, though the methodology is scalable.
The comparable performance between randomly selected modules and community-specific fine-tuning reveals a complex interplay between module specialization and task performance that requires further investigation.
future_direction: Explore network-wide dependencies, inter-layer connectivity, and adaptive optimization strategies that harness the model’s distributed learning potential more effectively.
Investigate the subtleties of modular interactions and the inherent flexibility of LLMs.
Apply the proposed methodology to larger architectures and datasets.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have reshaped our world with significant advancements in science, engineering, and society through applications ranging from scientific discoveries and medical diagnostics to Chatbots. Despite their ubiquity and utility, the underlying mechanisms of LLM remain concealed within billions of parameters and complex structures, making their inner architecture and cognitive processes challenging to comprehend. We address this gap by adopting approaches to understanding emerging cognition in biology and developing a network-based framework that links cognitive skills, LLM architectures, and datasets, ushering in a paradigm shift in foundation model analysis. The skill distribution in the module communities demonstrates that while LLMs do not strictly parallel the focalized specialization observed in specific biological systems, they exhibit unique communities of modules whose emergent skill patterns partially mirror the distributed yet interconnected cognitive organization seen in avian and small mammalian brains. Our numerical results highlight a key divergence from biological systems to LLMs, where skill acquisition benefits substantially from dynamic, cross-regional interactions and neural plasticity. By integrating cognitive science principles with machine learning, our framework provides new insights into LLM interpretability and suggests that effective fine-tuning strategies should leverage distributed learning dynamics rather than rigid modular interventions.

papers.title: Interpretability in Parameter Space: Minimizing Mechanistic Description Length with Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition
papers.research_question: How can we decompose neural network parameters into faithful, minimal, and simple mechanistic components?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components that are faithful, minimal, and simple, optimizing for minimal description length.
papers.conclusion: APD offers a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability, suggesting solutions to open problems like identifying minimal circuits in superposition and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition, though challenges remain for scaling.
papers.key_findings:
APD successfully recovers ground truth mechanisms in a toy model of superposition, decomposing the weight matrix into columns corresponding to individual features.
APD identifies parameter components representing individual functions in a toy model of compressed computation, where the model computes more nonlinear functions than it has neurons.
APD learns components that represent individual functions even when they span multiple layers in a toy model of cross-layer distributed representations.
APD's components are faithful to the original parameters, minimal in number per input, and simple in terms of rank.
papers.limitation:
High computational cost due to the need for multiple forward and backward passes.
Sensitivity to hyperparameters, such as the batch top-k value and loss coefficients.
Attributions are approximated using gradients, which may not perfectly capture causal importance.
future_direction: Improving computational cost
Improving robustness to hyperparameters
Improving attributions
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to understand the internal mechanisms learned by neural networks. Despite recent progress toward this goal, it remains unclear how best to decompose neural network parameters into mechanistic components. We introduce Attribution-based Parameter Decomposition (APD), a method that directly decomposes a neural network's parameters into components that (i) are faithful to the parameters of the original network, (ii) require a minimal number of components to process any input, and (iii) are maximally simple. Our approach thus optimizes for a minimal length description of the network's mechanisms. We demonstrate APD's effectiveness by successfully identifying ground truth mechanisms in multiple toy experimental settings: Recovering features from superposition; separating compressed computations; and identifying cross-layer distributed representations. While challenges remain to scaling APD to non-toy models, our results suggest solutions to several open problems in mechanistic interpretability, including identifying minimal circuits in superposition, offering a conceptual foundation for 'features', and providing an architecture-agnostic framework for neural network decomposition.

papers.title: Building artificial neural circuits for domain-general cognition: a primer on brain-inspired systems-level architecture
papers.research_question: How can principles from the brain's systems-level architecture, specifically recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes, inform the design of artificial neural networks for domain-general cognition?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reviews three brain-inspired architectural principles (global recurrence, communicability, and short-term topological changes) that could serve as inductive biases for building artificial neural networks capable of domain-general cognition.
papers.conclusion: A systems-level view of the brain, focusing on recurrence, communication, and rapid structural changes, can provide valuable guidance for building artificial intelligence that achieves domain-general problem-solving, and testing these principles in artificial systems may help understand biological cognition.
papers.key_findings:
The brain's Multiple Demand system uses global recurrence to integrate and broadcast information across distributed regions, a feature that may be necessary for domain-general cognition in artificial systems.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale networks can improve information flow between modules, which is crucial for complex multimodal systems.
Short-term topological changes (e.g., via local learning rules) enable flexible reconfiguration of neural circuits, supporting rapid adaptation and abstract problem-solving.
Current artificial neural networks lack these system-level properties, and incorporating them could enhance their flexibility and generalization.
future_direction: Incorporating global recurrent loops into artificial neural networks to enable widespread integration and broadcasting of abstract knowledge.
Optimizing communicability in large-scale modular networks to improve information flow between components.
Enabling short-term topological changes through local learning rules to allow rapid reconfiguration and flexible problem-solving.
papers.abstract: There is a concerted effort to build domain-general artificial intelligence in the form of universal neural network models with sufficient computational flexibility to solve a wide variety of cognitive tasks but without requiring fine-tuning on individual problem spaces and domains. To do this, models need appropriate priors and inductive biases, such that trained models can generalise to out-of-distribution examples and new problem sets. Here we provide an overview of the hallmarks endowing biological neural networks with the functionality needed for flexible cognition, in order to establish which features might also be important to achieve similar functionality in artificial systems. We specifically discuss the role of system-level distribution of network communication and recurrence, in addition to the role of short-term topological changes for efficient local computation. As machine learning models become more complex, these principles may provide valuable directions in an otherwise vast space of possible architectures. In addition, testing these inductive biases within artificial systems may help us to understand the biological principles underlying domain-general cognition.

papers.title: Mechanistic Unveiling of Transformer Circuits: Self-Influence as a Key to Model Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models perform multi-step reasoning? The paper aims to uncover the reasoning mechanisms (thought processes) used by language models in complex reasoning tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Self-Influence Circuit Analysis Framework (SICAF), which combines circuit analysis and self-influence functions to trace and analyze the reasoning pathways of language models, demonstrating its application on GPT-2 for the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that SICAF successfully maps reasoning pathways in language models, revealing a hierarchical reasoning structure similar to human thought processes.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed SICAF framework can trace the thought process of language models during complex reasoning tasks.
Circuits identified by EAP-IG and EAP-IG-KL are more faithful and compact than those identified by EAP.
The model's key parameters are concentrated in the first and last few layers.
The reasoning process follows a hierarchical structure: early layers identify entities, middle layers interpret actions, and final layers synthesize information.
Self-influence scores show how token importance changes across layers, revealing the reasoning path.
papers.limitation:
The analysis was conducted primarily on the GPT-2 model and may not generalize to larger or different architectures without adaptation.
Calculating self-influence requires computationally intensive methods, which may pose scalability challenges for more complex models.
Our work focused on a single task (Indirect Object Identification, or IOI), and the applicability of these findings to other natural language processing tasks remains an open question.
future_direction: Explore the adaptability of this approach across varied tasks and model architectures
Investigate methods to optimize computational efficiency
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models have achieved significant success; however, their internal mechanisms remain largely opaque due to the complexity of non-linear interactions and high-dimensional operations. While previous studies have demonstrated that these models implicitly embed reasoning trees, humans typically employ various distinct logical reasoning mechanisms to complete the same task. It is still unclear which multi-step reasoning mechanisms are used by language models to solve such tasks. In this paper, we aim to address this question by investigating the mechanistic interpretability of language models, particularly in the context of multi-step reasoning tasks. Specifically, we employ circuit analysis and self-influence functions to evaluate the changing importance of each token throughout the reasoning process, allowing us to map the reasoning paths adopted by the model. We apply this methodology to the GPT-2 model on a prediction task (IOI) and demonstrate that the underlying circuits reveal a human-interpretable reasoning process used by the model.

papers.title: Neuron to Graph: Interpreting Language Model Neurons at Scale
papers.research_question: How can we automatically interpret the behavior of individual neurons in large language models at scale?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Neuron to Graph (N2G), an automated method to convert neurons in LLMs into interpretable graph representations that capture neuron behavior, enabling visualization, automatic evaluation, and search for neurons with specific properties.
papers.conclusion: N2G is a step towards scalable interpretability for LLMs, enabling new forms of analysis like searching and comparing neurons, though it has limitations in capturing complex behavior in later layers.
papers.key_findings:
N2G produces interpretable graphs for neurons that can predict neuron activations with higher F1 score than simple lookup baselines.
The method works better for early layers than later layers due to increasing complexity of neuron behavior in deeper layers.
The graphs can be used to search for neurons with specific properties, e.g., an in-context learning neuron that activates on repeated token sequences.
The graphs can be compared to identify similar neurons, revealing pairs of neurons with identical behavior across layers.
The method scales to all neurons in a 6-layer Transformer model using a single Tesla T4 GPU.
papers.limitation:
Neuron graphs capture neuron behaviour well for early layers but only partially for later layers due to increasingly complex neuron behaviour.
The greater prevalence of polysemantic neurons in typical Transformer models could reduce the ability of N2G to fully capture neuron behaviour.
future_direction: Using more training examples to better cover the full extent of a neuron’s behaviour, better exploring the input space via more sophisticated and extensive augmentation, and generalising from exact token matches to matching abstract concepts (e.g., using token embeddings).
Using the graph representations to automatically identify circuits of neurons within LLMs that together perform a particular task.
papers.abstract: Advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have led to remarkable capabilities, yet their inner mechanisms remain largely unknown. To understand these models, we need to unravel the functions of individual neurons and their contribution to the network. This paper introduces a novel automated approach designed to scale interpretability techniques across a vast array of neurons within LLMs, to make them more interpretable and ultimately safe. Conventional methods require examination of examples with strong neuron activation and manual identification of patterns to decipher the concepts a neuron responds to. We propose Neuron to Graph (N2G), an innovative tool that automatically extracts a neuron's behaviour from the dataset it was trained on and translates it into an interpretable graph. N2G uses truncation and saliency methods to emphasise only the most pertinent tokens to a neuron while enriching dataset examples with diverse samples to better encompass the full spectrum of neuron behaviour. These graphs can be visualised to aid researchers' manual interpretation, and can generate token activations on text for automatic validation by comparison with the neuron's ground truth activations, which we use to show that the model is better at predicting neuron activation than two baseline methods. We also demonstrate how the generated graph representations can be flexibly used to facilitate further automation of interpretability research, by searching for neurons with particular properties, or programmatically comparing neurons to each other to identify similar neurons. Our method easily scales to build graph representations for all neurons in a 6-layer Transformer model using a single Tesla T4 GPU, allowing for wide usability. We release the code and instructions for use at https://github.com/alexjfoote/Neuron2Graph.

papers.title: Wider Networks Learn Better Features
papers.research_question: How does network width affect the features learned by neural networks, and do wider networks learn more transferable features for novel tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Wider networks learn more informative and transferable features in their hidden states, as visualized by activation atlases, leading to better performance when fine-tuning on novel tasks, even when test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.
papers.conclusion: Wider networks learn more informative features that are beneficial for transfer learning, even when original task performance is unchanged.
papers.key_findings:
Individual neurons in wide networks do not learn interpretable features, but groups of neurons (via activation atlases) do.
Hidden states of wide networks contain more information about inputs than narrow networks, even when test accuracy on the original task is the same.
Fine-tuning a linear classifier on features from a wide network on a new task yields better performance than on narrow networks, even with the same original task accuracy.
The additional information in wide networks (e.g., translation information in translated MNIST) is preserved and useful for transfer.
The features learned by wide networks are distributed across neurons, not sparse.
papers.limitation:
Hyperparameters for wider networks (e.g., learning rate) might be tuned to improve performance on the original task, but this was not explored.
The experiments are conducted on relatively small datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) and network widths, not in the infinite width or lazy training regime.
future_direction: Explore the effect of network width on the performance of transfer learning algorithms like MAML.
Investigate feature learning in the infinite width limit and lazy training regime.
papers.abstract: Transferability of learned features between tasks can massively reduce the cost of training a neural network on a novel task. We investigate the effect of network width on learned features using activation atlases --- a visualization technique that captures features the entire hidden state responds to, as opposed to individual neurons alone. We find that, while individual neurons do not learn interpretable features in wide networks, groups of neurons do. In addition, the hidden state of a wide network contains more information about the inputs than that of a narrow network trained to the same test accuracy. Inspired by this observation, we show that when fine-tuning the last layer of a network on a new task, performance improves significantly as the width of the network is increased, even though test accuracy on the original task is independent of width.

papers.title: Interpretable Risk Mitigation in LLM Agent Systems
papers.research_question: How can we align LLM agents with human values using interpretable features from sparse autoencoders in a game-theoretic setting?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to steer LLM agents' strategies in a game-theoretic environment using interpretable features from sparse autoencoders, effectively reducing defection probability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based steering can modulate LLM agent strategies in game-theoretic settings, and monosemantic features are promising for alignment.
papers.key_findings:
Steering with the 'sacrifice' feature reduces defection probability by 47 percentage points.
The 'good/bad faith' feature in LLaMA3-8B reduces defection probability by 28 percentage points and is monosemantic.
Different models (Gemma, Gemma2, LLaMA3) have different baseline defection probabilities and responses to steering.
Monosemantic features are more reliable for steering than polysemantic ones.
The range of achievable strategies via steering varies across models.
papers.limitation: Polysemantic features may lead to unintended side effects when used for steering.
future_direction: Scaling model size for better understanding and larger context windows.
Refining SAEs to increase monosemanticity and enable more precise steering.
Exploring multilayer steering and generalization to real-world applications.
papers.abstract: Autonomous agents powered by large language models (LLMs) enable novel use cases in domains where responsible action is increasingly important. Yet the inherent unpredictability of LLMs raises safety concerns about agent reliability. In this work, we explore agent behaviour in a toy, game-theoretic environment based on a variation of the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma. We introduce a strategy-modification method-independent of both the game and the prompt-by steering the residual stream with interpretable features extracted from a sparse autoencoder latent space. Steering with the good-faith negotiation feature lowers the average defection probability by 28 percentage points. We also identify feasible steering ranges for several open-source LLM agents. Finally, we hypothesise that game-theoretic evaluation of LLM agents, combined with representation-steering alignment, can generalise to real-world applications on end-user devices and embodied platforms.

papers.title: Comparing Bottom-Up and Top-Down Steering Approaches on In-Context Learning Tasks
papers.research_question: What is the comparative effectiveness of bottom-up (function vectors) and top-down (in-context vectors) steering approaches on diverse in-context learning tasks, and under what conditions does each method excel?
papers.core_contribution: Bottom-up function vectors excel at precise functional tasks but struggle with behavioral shifts, while top-down in-context vectors are effective for behavioral shifts but less reliable for precise tasks, highlighting complementary strengths and limitations of the two steering approaches.
papers.conclusion: Both bottom-up and top-down steering methods are effective only on specific types of in-context learning tasks and cannot fully replace in-context learning, highlighting the need for a unified evaluation benchmark and better understanding of in-context learning mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Function vectors (FVs) outperform in-context vectors (ICVs) on all functional tasks (antonym, capitalize, country-capital, synonym) across zero-shot, few-shot, and natural text settings.
In-context vectors (ICVs) outperform function vectors (FVs) on behavioral tasks (detoxification, sentiment transfer), but with high variance and sensitivity to demonstration data.
ICVs are prone to causing fluency degradation and are less robust when applied in different contexts, while FVs generalize better to out-of-distribution settings.
FV performance is strongly correlated with the causal indirect effect (CIE) of attention heads, indicating that FVs rely on the existence of attention heads that significantly affect task performance.
Both steering methods have significant limitations and cannot serve as a general substitute for in-context learning, emphasizing the need for a unified evaluation benchmark.
papers.limitation:
The study only compares FVs and ICVs on a relatively small set of functional and behavioral tasks, so results may not generalize to an expanded set of tasks.
The work only considers two steering methods, so findings may not generalize to all bottom-up or top-down approaches for vector steering or interpretability.
future_direction: Expanding the scope of the study to other tasks, models, and steering methods.
Developing explanations for the variable performance of FVs and ICVs to improve understanding of in-context learning in LLMs.
papers.abstract: A key objective of interpretability research on large language models (LLMs) is to develop methods for robustly steering models toward desired behaviors. To this end, two distinct approaches to interpretability -- ``bottom-up" and ``top-down" -- have been presented, but there has been little quantitative comparison between them. We present a case study comparing the effectiveness of representative vector steering methods from each branch: function vectors (FV; arXiv:2310.15213), as a bottom-up method, and in-context vectors (ICV; arXiv:2311.06668) as a top-down method. While both aim to capture compact representations of broad in-context learning tasks, we find they are effective only on specific types of tasks: ICVs outperform FVs in behavioral shifting, whereas FVs excel in tasks requiring more precision. We discuss the implications for future evaluations of steering methods and for further research into top-down and bottom-up steering given these findings.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: InterPLM: Discovering Interpretable Features in Protein Language Models via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.abstract: A bstract Protein language models (PLMs) have demonstrated remarkable success in protein modeling and design, yet their internal mechanisms for predicting structure and function remain poorly understood. Here we present a systematic approach to extract and analyze interpretable features from PLMs using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). By training SAEs on embeddings from the PLM ESM-2, we identify thousands of human-interpretable latent features per layer that highlight hundreds of known biological concepts such as binding sites, structural motifs, and functional domains. In contrast, examining individual neurons in ESM-2 reveals significantly less conceptual alignment, suggesting that PLMs represent most concepts in superposition. We further demonstrate that a larger PLM (ESM-2 with 650M parameters) captures substantially more interpretable concepts than a smaller PLM (ESM-2 with 8M parameters). Beyond capturing known annotations, we show that ESM-2 learns coherent concepts that do not map onto existing annotations and propose a pipeline using language models to automatically interpret novel latent features learned by the SAEs. As practical applications, we demonstrate how these latent features can fill in missing annotations in protein databases and enable targeted steering of protein sequence generation. Our results demonstrate that PLMs encode rich, interpretable representations of protein biology and we propose a systematic framework to uncover and understand these latent features. In the process, we recover both known biology and potentially new protein motifs. As community resources, we introduce InterPLM (interPLM.ai), an interactive visualization platform for investigating learned PLM features, and release code for training and analysis at github.com/ElanaPearl/interPLM.

papers.title: ProteinReasoner: A Multi-Modal Protein Language Model with Chain-of-Thought Reasoning for Efficient Protein Design
papers.abstract: Abstract Protein language models (PLMs) have advanced the understanding and engineering of proteins by learning rich representations from large-scale sequence data. However, sequence-only models are limited in their ability to capture structural and evolutionary constraints essential for protein tasks. Although recent multi-modal PLMs integrate sequence and structure, they often fail to explicitly model the stepwise reasoning processes fundamental to protein science, particularly the evolutionary constraints and decision-making logic critical for protein design and optimization. Here, we introduce ProteinReasoner, a multi-modal protein language model that explicitly incorporates the “evolutionary profile” as the intermediate reasoning step between structure and sequence modalities within a chain-of-thought (CoT) framework. We demonstrated that ProteinReasoner achieved improved zero-shot performance in structure prediction, inverse protein folding, and fitness prediction tasks, consistently outperforming larger baselines including ESM3 and DPLM-2. Furthermore, we developed a novel In-context learning (ICL) paradigm for protein optimization that leverages ProteinReasoner’s reasoning capabilities to guide sequence generation based on prior experimental feedback. ProteinReasoner outperformed the conventional active learning paradigm in protein optimization tasks, achieving higher predictive accuracy and better generalization. ProteinReasoner offers a scalable, efficient, and generalizable framework for protein modeling and optimization, providing a practical path to accelerate protein engineering workflows and enhance mechanistic understanding of protein biology.

papers.title: Feature Reuse and Scaling: Understanding Transfer Learning with Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Abstract Large pretrained protein language models (PLMs) have improved protein property and structure prediction from sequences via transfer learning, in which weights and representations from PLMs are repurposed for downstream tasks. Although PLMs have shown great promise, currently there is little understanding of how the features learned by pretraining relate to and are useful for downstream tasks. We perform a systematic analysis of transfer learning using PLMs, conducting 370 experiments across a comprehensive suite of factors including different downstream tasks, architectures, model sizes, model depths, and pretraining time. We observe that while almost all down-stream tasks do benefit from pretrained models compared to naive sequence representations, for the majority of tasks performance does not scale with pretraining, and instead relies on low-level features learned early in pretraining. Our results point to a mismatch between current PLM pretraining paradigms and most applications of these models, indicating a need for better pretraining methods.

papers.title: Sparse autoencoders uncover biologically interpretable features in protein language model representations
papers.abstract: Foundation models in biology-particularly protein language models (PLMs)-have enabled ground-breaking predictions in protein structure, function, and beyond. However, the "black-box" nature of these representations limits transparency and explainability, posing challenges for human-AI collaboration and leaving open questions about their human-interpretable features. Here, we leverage sparse autoencoders (SAEs) and a variant, transcoders, from natural language processing to extract, in a completely unsupervised fashion, interpretable sparse features present in both protein-level and amino acid (AA)-level representations from ESM2, a popular PLM. Unlike other approaches such as training probes for features, the extraction of features by the SAE is performed without any supervision. We find that many sparse features extracted from SAEs trained on protein-level representations are tightly associated with Gene Ontology (GO) terms across all levels of the GO hierarchy. We also use Anthropic's Claude to automate the interpretation of sparse features for both protein-level and AA-level representations and find that many of these features correspond to specific protein families and functions such as the NAD Kinase, IUNH, and the PTH family, as well as proteins involved in methyltransferase activity and in olfactory and gustatory sensory perception. We show that sparse features are more interpretable than ESM2 neurons across all our trained SAEs and transcoders. These findings demonstrate that SAEs offer a promising unsupervised approach for disentangling biologically relevant information present in PLM representations, thus aiding interpretability. This work opens the door to safety, trust, and explainability of PLMs and their applications, and paves the way to extracting meaningful biological insights across increasingly powerful models in the life sciences.

papers.title: Biophysics-based protein language models for protein engineering
papers.abstract: Protein language models trained on evolutionary data have emerged as powerful tools for predictive problems involving protein sequence, structure, and function. However, these models overlook decades of research into biophysical factors governing protein function. We propose Mutational Effect Transfer Learning (METL), a protein language model framework that unites advanced machine learning and biophysical modeling. Using the METL framework, we pretrain transformer-based neural networks on biophysical simulation data to capture fundamental relationships between protein sequence, structure, and energetics. We finetune METL on experimental sequence-function data to harness these biophysical signals and apply them when predicting protein properties like thermostability, catalytic activity, and fluorescence. METL excels in challenging protein engineering tasks like generalizing from small training sets and position extrapolation, although existing methods that train on evolutionary signals remain powerful for many types of experimental assays. We demonstrate METL's ability to design functional green fluorescent protein variants when trained on only 64 examples, showcasing the potential of biophysics-based protein language models for protein engineering.

papers.title: Guiding Generative Models for Protein Design: Prompting, Steering and Aligning
papers.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) models learn probability distributions from data and produce novel samples that capture the salient properties of their training sets. Proteins are particularly attractive for such approaches given their abundant data and the versatility of their representations, ranging from sequences to structures and functions. This versatility has motivated the rapid development of generative models for protein design, enabling the generation of functional proteins and enzymes with unprecedented success. However, because these models mirror their training distribution, they tend to sample from its most probable modes, while low-probability regions, often encoding valuable properties, remain underexplored. To address this challenge, recent work has focused on guiding generative models to produce proteins with user-specified properties, even when such properties are rare or absent from the original training distribution. In this review, we survey and categorize recent advances in conditioning generative models for protein design. We distinguish approaches that modify model parameters, such as reinforcement learning or supervised fine-tuning, from those that keep the model fixed, including conditional generation, retrieval-augmented strategies, Bayesian guidance, and tailored sampling methods. Together, these developments are beginning to enable the steering of generative models toward proteins with desired, and often previously inaccessible, properties.

papers.title: The promises of large language models for protein design and modeling
papers.abstract: The recent breakthroughs of Large Language Models (LLMs) in the context of natural language processing have opened the way to significant advances in protein research. Indeed, the relationships between human natural language and the "language of proteins" invite the application and adaptation of LLMs to protein modelling and design. Considering the impressive results of GPT-4 and other recently developed LLMs in processing, generating and translating human languages, we anticipate analogous results with the language of proteins. Indeed, protein language models have been already trained to accurately predict protein properties, generate novel functionally characterized proteins, achieving state-of-the-art results. In this paper we discuss the promises and the open challenges raised by this novel and exciting research area, and we propose our perspective on how LLMs will affect protein modeling and design.

papers.title: From Mechanistic Interpretability to Mechanistic Biology: Training, Evaluating, and Interpreting Sparse Autoencoders on Protein Language Models
papers.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful predictors of protein structure and function, learning through unsupervised training on millions of protein sequences. pLMs are thought to capture common motifs in protein sequences, but the specifics of pLM features are not well understood. Identifying these features would not only shed light on how pLMs work, but potentially uncover novel protein biology--studying the model to study the biology. Motivated by this, we train sparse autoencoders (SAEs) on the residual stream of a pLM, ESM-2. By characterizing SAE features, we determine that pLMs use a combination of generic features and family-specific features to represent a protein. In addition, we demonstrate how known sequence determinants of properties such as thermostability and subcellular localization can be identified by linear probing of SAE features. For predictive features without known functional associations, we hypothesize their role in unknown mechanisms and provide visualization tools to aid their interpretation. Our study gives a better understanding of the limitations of pLMs, and demonstrates how SAE features can be used to help generate hypotheses for biological mechanisms. We release our code, model weights and feature visualizer.

papers.title: A Benchmarking Platform for Assessing Protein Language Models on Function-related Prediction Tasks
papers.abstract: Abstract Proteins play a crucial role in almost all biological processes, serving as the building blocks of life and mediating various cellular functions, from enzymatic reactions to immune responses. Accurate annotation of protein functions is essential for advancing our understanding of biological systems and developing innovative biotechnological applications and therapeutic strategies. To predict protein function, researchers primarily rely on classical homology-based methods, which use evolutionary relationships, and increasingly on machine learning (ML) approaches. Lately, protein language models (PLMs) have gained prominence; these models leverage specialised deep learning architectures to effectively capture intricate relationships between sequence, structure, and function. We recently conducted a comprehensive benchmarking study to evaluate diverse protein representations (i.e., classical approaches and PLMs) and discuss their trade-offs. The current work introduces the Protein Representation Benchmark – PROBE tool, a benchmarking framework designed to evaluate protein representations on function-related prediction tasks. Here, we provide a detailed protocol for running the framework via the GitHub repository and accessing our newly developed user-friendly web service. PROBE encompasses four core tasks: semantic similarity inference, ontology-based function prediction, drug target family classification, and protein-protein binding affinity estimation. We demonstrate PROBE’s usage through a new use case evaluating ESM2 and three recent multimodal PLMs—ESM3, ProstT5, and SaProt—highlighting their ability to integrate diverse data types, including sequence and structural information. This study underscores the potential of protein language models in advancing protein function prediction and serves as a valuable tool for both PLM developers and users.

papers.title: Codon language embeddings provide strong signals for use in protein engineering
papers.abstract: Abstract Protein representations from deep language models have yielded state-of-the-art performance across many tasks in computational protein engineering. In recent years, progress has primarily focused on parameter count, with recent models’ capacities surpassing the size of the very datasets they were trained on. Here we propose an alternative direction. We show that large language models trained on codons, instead of amino acid sequences, provide high-quality representations that outperform comparable state-of-the-art models across a variety of tasks.
